name: The Nation cryptic crossword No 3417
preamble: Puzzled? No more cross words! Read Kosman and Picciotto on “Solving The Nation’s Cryptic Puzzles.” Or watch this video.

clue.text: Something representative of the era: ?

blocks.note: surface reading: a token that sums up the present age
setter's reading: the bare question mark is itself the token, a symbol of how uncertain the present feels

explanation.surface: A puzzle asks what object best captures our age, and offers only a shrug of punctuation.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue is the phrase plus a lone question mark: the punctuation is offered as the emblem of an uncertain era (the puzzle ran just after the 2016 US election).
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom names any development typical of the present period, which is exactly what the first half of the clue describes.

clue.text: Start to snore quietly, missing a very loud kind of TV show

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter, so that one letter is taken
missing means lacking, so the following single letter is dropped from the word before it

blocks.note: the opening letter of the word
piano is the musical direction to play softly
the letter that goes missing
ff, fortissimo, is the musical direction for very loud

explanation.surface: A dozing viewer drifts off quietly, but not during a blaring programme.
explanation.walkthrough: Both 'quietly' and 'very loud' are musical markings: piano for soft, ff for fortissimo.
explanation.definitionFit: A spin-off is a television series built around characters or a setting taken from an earlier show.

clue.text: Guard's ID badge, upside down

indicators.note: in a down entry, turning a word upside down puts its last letter at the top

blocks.note: a name tag is a badge showing who you are

explanation.surface: A security guard's identity badge has been pinned on the wrong way up.
explanation.definitionFit: A gateman is a person posted at a gate to control who enters, a kind of guard.

clue.text: Monster is so withdrawn

indicators.note: something withdrawn is drawn back, so the word is taken backwards

blocks.note: ergo is Latin for therefore, so

explanation.surface: A beast that turns out to be shy and retiring.
explanation.definitionFit: An ogre is a man-eating giant of folklore, a classic fairy-tale monster.

clue.text: Become a coffeepot coated with color orange

indicators.note: a thing coated with something is wrapped in it, so one piece goes round the other

blocks.note: a tint is a shade of colour
an urn is a large vessel for serving coffee or tea
O stands for orange in the colour sequence ROYGBIV

explanation.surface: An instruction to transform into a coffee urn painted bright orange.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Become a coffeepot' reads as one instruction, but the definition is 'Become' alone; 'a coffeepot' is the vessel inside the colour.
explanation.definitionFit: To turn into something is to change and become it, as a caterpillar turns into a butterfly.

clue.text: Inherently complex tolerance for praise

indicators.note: something present inherently is contained within, so the letters sit inside the words that follow

blocks.note: the letters run across the join of the two words

explanation.surface: A tangled capacity for accepting compliments, as a psychologist might describe it.
explanation.definitionFit: To extol someone is to praise them highly and enthusiastically.

clue.text: Charge from the subcontinent covering Treasury Department agents' time

indicators.note: in a down entry, one piece covering another sits on top of it, so it comes first

blocks.note: Indic means of India and its languages
T-men were US Treasury agents
T is the standard abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: An Indian fee levied to pay for federal agents' working hours.
explanation.definitionFit: A charge in law is a formal accusation, which is what an indictment sets out.

clue.text: "There's a mouse," a restaurant staffer said, "that's as far as possible from the poles"

definitions.text: that's as far as possible from the poles
definitions.note: a relative clause standing for the noun it describes, the line that is

indicators.note: said means spoken, so the words count for their sound rather than their spelling

blocks.note: the shriek someone gives on seeing a mouse
a waiter serves tables in a restaurant

explanation.surface: A diner spots a mouse and calls out to the waiter, who offers a geography fact.
explanation.walkthrough: The cry 'Eek, waiter!' run together is the sound of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The great circle around the Earth's middle lies halfway between North and South Poles, the farthest any point can be from both.

clue.text: Scientist: "Lend me bananas"

indicators.note: bananas is slang for crazy, so the letters go wild and rearrange

blocks.note: the two words used letter for letter

explanation.surface: A researcher asks to borrow some fruit for an experiment.
explanation.definitionFit: Gregor Mendel was the monk and scientist whose pea-plant experiments founded genetics.

clue.text: Read letters from Pinter, some more than once

indicators.note: the answer is built out of the letters of the name, taken in a new order rather than as spelt

blocks.note: Harold Pinter, the playwright, supplies the letter stock
three of the name's letters are used a second time

explanation.surface: A reader works through Harold Pinter's correspondence, going over some passages repeatedly.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the six letters of PINTER are used; R, E and T each appear twice in INTERPRET, which is what 'some more than once' allows.
explanation.definitionFit: To read something can mean to construe its meaning, as in reading a situation, which is a synonym of interpreting it.

clue.text: Get wet to perform at benefit

blocks.note: to do a play or a turn is to perform it
use as in 'of no use', an advantage or benefit

explanation.surface: A performer at a charity benefit agrees to be soaked for the cause.
explanation.definitionFit: Here the answer is used in the sense of drench: to soak someone or something with liquid makes it wet.

clue.text: Leads in opera house might sense some resistance

indicators.note: the leads of a group of words are their front letters, so only the initials are kept

blocks.note: initial letters of the four words

explanation.surface: The stars of an opera company might feel some opposition building backstage.
explanation.definitionFit: Electrical resistance is measured in units named after Georg Ohm, so a quantity of them is some resistance.

clue.text: After accident, date is cold and out of joint

indicators.note: an accident leaves things smashed and jumbled, so the words that follow are scrambled

blocks.note: the three words used letter for letter

explanation.surface: After a crash, a dinner companion is chilly and has a joint knocked loose.
explanation.definitionFit: A dislocated shoulder or hip has had the bone pushed out of its socket, literally out of joint.

clue.text: Playwright is keen on classic Broadway musical during downtime

indicators.note: something happening during a period falls within it, so these pieces go inside

blocks.note: split as down and time, abbreviated D and T
avid means eager or keen
Mame, the 1966 Jerry Herman show

explanation.surface: A dramatist loves an old Broadway hit and watches it in his spare time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Downtime' looks like one word but splits into its two abbreviations, D and T, which go round the other pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: David Mamet is the American dramatist of Glengarry Glen Ross and American Buffalo.

clue.text: Close to interrupting convulsions with creative endeavors

indicators.note: to interrupt something is to break into the middle of it, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: fits are spasms or convulsions
near means close to

explanation.surface: Someone almost breaks off in spasms brought on by their artistic efforts.
explanation.definitionFit: Painting, sculpture, music and the like are the fine arts, the classic fields of creative work.

clue.text: Morning test is value-free

blocks.note: a.m. marks the hours before noon
an oral is a spoken examination

explanation.surface: A dawn exam turns out to carry no weight at all.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone amoral has no moral values at all, so their conduct is free of any value system.

clue.text: To have a different opinion is a sin, after putting the end at the beginning

indicators.text: after putting the end at the beginning
indicators.note: moving a final letter round to the front rotates the string by one place

blocks.note: taken as written
greed is one of the seven deadly sins

explanation.surface: Holding a dissenting view counts as wrongdoing, according to some dogma.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Is a sin' reads as a statement, but 'sin' is GREED; the D at its end moves to the front of the whole string.
explanation.definitionFit: To disagree is to hold a view that differs from someone else's.

clue.text: "Buzz off, laird," Scotsman concluded

indicators.note: something off is out of order or not right, so the letters are rearranged
what concludes a word is its final letter, so just that letter is kept

blocks.note: a laird is a Scottish landowner; used letter for letter
the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A Scottish landowner is brusquely told to go away, and the Scotsman ends the conversation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Buzz off' reads as a dismissal, but Buzz alone is the definition, the astronaut's first name, and 'off' scrambles the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Buzz is the nickname of Edwin Aldrin, the second astronaut to walk on the Moon.

clue.text: Look — fruit under a piano

indicators.note: in a down entry, what is placed under something comes after it

blocks.note: taken as written
p is the musical marking for piano, softly
a common fruit

explanation.surface: Someone points out a piece of fruit that has rolled beneath the piano.
explanation.definitionFit: To look a certain way is to appear so, as in 'she looks tired'.

clue.text: Bad rule, regrettably, is likely to last

indicators.note: things that go regrettably have gone wrong, so the letters before it come out in the wrong order

blocks.note: the two words used letter for letter

explanation.surface: A bad law, sadly, will probably be around for a long time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bad' looks like the shuffle signal, but it is part of the fodder; 'regrettably' is what tells you the letters have gone wrong.
explanation.definitionFit: Durable things withstand wear and time, so they are expected to last.

clue.text: Don't waste time casually circling hotel with a spice

indicators.note: circling something goes all round it, so one part wraps around the other

blocks.note: c'mon, a casual 'come on', urges someone to hurry
an inn is a small hotel
taken as written

explanation.surface: A traveller hustles around a hotel in search of a seasoning.
explanation.definitionFit: The bark of a tropical tree, ground or rolled into sticks, is one of the most familiar baking spices.

clue.text: Steve and I get a drink

blocks.note: Steve Martin, the comic actor
taken as written

explanation.surface: Two friends, one named Steve, head to the bar for a round.
explanation.definitionFit: A martini is a cocktail of gin or vodka with vermouth.

clue.text: Male relative swaps two for one before showing subatomic particle

indicators.note: the two letters that spell 'one' in French trade places, so that pair is flipped

blocks.note: a parent's brother
a film that is showing is on

explanation.surface: An uncle trades in a pair of things for one, then shows off a tiny particle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Two for one' sounds like a bargain, but 'one' here is French: UN, whose two letters change places at the front of the relative.
explanation.definitionFit: A nucleon is either of the particles in an atomic nucleus, a proton or a neutron.

clue.text: Hothead overheard one with a passion for Greek letters?

indicators.note: something overheard is caught by ear, so the phrase is judged on how it is spoken

blocks.clueFragment: one with a passion for Greek letters
blocks.note: pi and rho are Greek letters; a maniac has a passion for them

explanation.surface: A quick-tempered type is overheard talking about a fan of the Greek alphabet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hothead' usually means a short temper; here it is someone literally obsessed with fire.
explanation.definitionFit: A playful definition: a person with a compulsion to set fires is hot-headed in the most literal sense.

clue.text: Anaïs seen on Jamaica's shores with a highly trained Japanese spy

indicators.note: an island's shores are its outer edges, so only the outside letters are kept

blocks.note: Anaïs Nin, the diarist and author
the first and last letters of the island's name

explanation.surface: The writer Anaïs Nin is spotted on a Jamaican beach alongside a covert agent from Japan.
explanation.definitionFit: Ninjas were the trained covert agents and assassins of feudal Japan.

clue.text: Idle group of doctors abandoning our country

indicators.note: abandoning something means leaving it behind, so those letters drop out of the word

blocks.note: the setters' country, The Nation being a US magazine
the American Medical Association

explanation.surface: Lazy physicians are accused of deserting the nation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Idle' looks like an adjective, but it is a surname: the definition is the Monty Python member, and the answer is his first name. AMA is removed from the start and end of AMERICA.
explanation.definitionFit: Eric is the first name of Idle, the Monty Python comedian, so the surname leads to the given name.

clue.text: Indigenous people can advance frontally

indicators.note: frontally means at the front, so just the opening letter is used

blocks.note: may means can, in the sense of being allowed
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: Native peoples are able to push forward with a frontal assault.
explanation.definitionFit: The Maya are the Indigenous people of southern Mexico and Central America.

clue.text: Record a large slacker

blocks.note: taken as written
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large
a bum is an idler or loafer

explanation.surface: A note is made of one particularly big layabout.
explanation.definitionFit: An album is a long-playing record, a collection of tracks released together.

clue.text: Story of Madonna film, with happier ending, broadcast in reverse

indicators.note: the ending of a word is its last letter, so only that letter is used
in reverse means back to front, so the assembled string is read from right to left

blocks.note: Madonna starred in the 1996 film of the musical
the last letter of the word
a programme that was broadcast ran on air

explanation.surface: A tale about a Madonna movie, rewritten with a cheerier ending and aired backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A narrative is an account of connected events, which is what a story is.

clue.text: Supergiant contributions arranged for old person

indicators.note: arranged means put into a new order, so the letters are reordered

blocks.note: ten of the fourteen letters, used letter for letter
these are the four letters still needed, but no standard sense of this word gives them; the setters' intended reading is unclear

explanation.surface: A giant star's offerings are put in order for someone elderly.
explanation.walkthrough: SUPERGIANT supplies ten letters, which is the heart of the anagram, but no ordinary reading of 'contributions' gives the A, A, E and N left over; the crossing letters confirm the answer regardless.
explanation.definitionFit: A septuagenarian is someone in their seventies, so an old person.
